title: Being counted
hook: showing up so a minyan can happen
tomorrow: Mr. Feld's in the hospital. visit and talk, or go and sweep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Honi woke to a world with no one he knew, and the saying it left: companionship or death. Find your people. Then comes the morning someone needs you to be one of them.

Seven in the morning, a small shul, and the group text says what it says too often: we have nine. Nine people can pray. What they can't do is say Kaddish, the mourner's prayer, or read from the Torah scroll in public. Those wait for ten. So where does ten come from? Here's the odd part. The Talmud finds it in the Torah's worst crowd: the spies who came back from Canaan and talked a whole people out of going in. God calls them, in the JPS 1917 translation, "this evil congregation."
screen: `WE HAVE NINE.` → `KADDISH WAITS FOR TEN.` → `"THIS EVIL CONGREGATION."`

segments.voice: Count the spies with the bad report. The Torah sends twelve, and two of them, Joshua and Caleb, disagree. That leaves ten, and the Torah calls those ten a congregation, an edah. The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, links that word to another verse, where God is made holy among the children of Israel. A congregation is ten, it reasons, so holiness in public needs ten. That ten is a minyan. Now the puzzle: why build a holy number on a bad crowd? One answer some teachers give is that a congregation was never a club of saints. It's people who show up, imperfect, and get counted. Who counts differs. In Orthodox synagogues, the ten are men past bar mitzvah; in egalitarian communities, women count as well. Either way, the tenth person isn't an extra. The mourner standing there can't say Kaddish for a parent until somebody else walks in. Something to tell a friend tonight: there's an old reluctance to count people by number, so some congregations count with a verse instead, a line from Psalms with ten Hebrew words, one word per person. It asks God to save the people and bless them. Nobody is a number. Each one is a word in a blessing.
screen: `TWELVE SPIES, TEN WITH A BAD REPORT.` · `A CONGREGATION IS TEN.` · `NOT SAINTS: PEOPLE WHO SHOW UP.` · `A WORD IN A BLESSING.` · then, large: `BE COUNTED.`

segments.voice: Stand up where you are, feet planted, as if you just walked through the door and made it ten. Feel your weight on the floor; that's what showing up weighs. Stay standing, and name one gathering this week where your being there could make the difference.
screen: `STAND, FEET PLANTED.` · `YOU MADE IT TEN.` · `ONE GATHERING THIS WEEK.`

segments.voice: Being counted: showing up so something holy can happen. Ten make a congregation, and the tenth matters as much as the first.
Hold onto this: be counted, because somewhere a mourner is waiting for ten. That's two days of community.

howItsDone: Many synagogues hold daily morning and evening services that need a minyan of ten for Kaddish and the Torah reading; members often sign up or get a call when a mourner needs the tenth person.

notes: Numbers 14:27: only the phrase 'this evil congregation' is quoted; confirm it matches JPS 1917.
Megillah 23b derivation summarized (edah of the ten spies; 'I will be hallowed among the children of Israel'). Confirm.

Psalm 28:9 has ten words in Hebrew (counted from the Masoretic text: hoshia et amecha u'varech et nachalatecha u're'em v'nas'em ad ha'olam); its use for counting a minyan is a custom, presented as 'some congregations'. Confirm.
Who counts toward a minyan: Orthodox (men past bar mitzvah) and egalitarian communities (women too), stated without ranking. Confirm framing.
'One answer some teachers give' (a congregation is not a club of saints) is a reading, not the Talmud's stated reason. Confirm framing.
